title: Construct Quad Tree
hints: the recursion needs three things: which sub-square of the grid you're looking at (top-left corner and size), and a way to check whether that sub-square is a single uniform value
write a helper that checks if every cell in a given r, c, size sub-square equals the same value - if so, emit a leaf immediately without recursing further

if the sub-square isn't uniform, recurse into the four half-sized sub-squares in top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right order, and splice their results together after the [0, -1] internal marker
the top-left corner of each child is (r, c), (r, c+half), (r+half, c), (r+half, c+half) where half = size / 2
build the output as one flat list, appending [0, -1] or [1, val] then recursively appending each child's flattened output right after, so the final array is a valid preorder serialization
commonMistakes: checking only the four corners of a quadrant for uniformity instead of every cell, which misses non-uniform interior cells
getting the top-left corner offsets wrong for the four children (mixing up which half of size applies to rows vs columns)
forgetting to emit the [0, -1] marker before the children's serializations, or emitting it after instead of in preorder position
not handling the base case where size is already 1 (always uniform, always a leaf)

content.problemStatement:
You're given an n x n binary grid (n is always a power of 2) of 0s and
1s. A quad tree represents this grid by recursively splitting it into
four equal quadrants whenever the quadrant isn't a single uniform color,
stopping and forming a leaf whenever every cell in a quadrant already
holds the same value.

Since there's no tree type in this problem set, return the quad tree as
a flat integer array, built by a preorder walk:

- a leaf quadrant emits the two values `[1, val]` - `1` marks "leaf", `val` is the uniform 0 or 1 it represents
- an internal (split) quadrant emits `[0, -1]` - `0` marks "internal", `-1` is a placeholder with no meaning - immediately followed, still within the same flat array and still in preorder, by the four serializations of its children in the order top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right

For example, `grid = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]` is not uniform, so the root splits into its four 1x1 quadrants, each trivially uniform:

```
top-left=0   top-right=1
bottom-left=1  bottom-right=0
```

It emits `[0, -1]`, then each quadrant's leaf in order: top-left `[1, 0]`, top-right `[1, 1]`, bottom-left `[1, 1]`, bottom-right `[1, 0]`. Concatenated, the full output is `[0, -1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0]`.

**Given `grid`, build its quad tree and return it as the flat preorder array described above.**
constraints: 1 <= n <= 64, and n is always a power of 2
every cell of grid is either 0 or 1
the recursion always bottoms out at 1x1 quadrants, which are uniform by definition
notes: a 1x1 grid (immediately a leaf, no splitting possible)
a fully uniform grid of any size (a single leaf at the root, no splitting at all)
a checkerboard pattern, which forces splitting all the way down to 1x1 leaves at every branch
a grid where only one quadrant needs further splitting while the other three are already uniform

optimal.time: O(n^2) with a uniformity check that can early-exit as soon as a mismatch is found
optimal.space: O(log n) recursion stack, plus O(n^2) output array in the worst case (a checkerboard, which splits all the way down)
optimal.pattern: divide and conquer: recursively split into four quadrants, short-circuiting to a leaf as soon as a quadrant is uniform

bruteForce.approach: for every quadrant considered, scan all of its cells to check if they're uniform before deciding whether to split - this is what the recursive solution already does at each level, there's no meaningfully different brute force
bruteForce.time: O(n^2 log n) since each of the O(log n) levels of recursion re-scans up to n^2 cells in total
bruteForce.space: O(log n) recursion stack, plus the output array
